newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia inflation,wages seen leading to rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Australia inflation,wages seen leading to rate cut.

text.p: Australia's second quarter inflation and wage data due next week should be bullish for those looking for a near term cut in official interest rates.

Underlying inflation is expected to fall to its lowest annual level since the series began in the early 1970s, while the consumer price index is expected to have been flat in the quarter and wages are expected to have shown further moderation.
Combined with a stalled labour market, subdued confidence and an economy running below capacity, the conditions seem ripe for a fifth rate cut from the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA).

"Given the weakness in June employment data and expectations for a further step down in the rate of underlying inflation in the June quarter, the RBA could move to cut rates another 50 basis points," ANZ Treasury economists said in a report.
The official cash rate currently stands at 5.50 percent. It has been cut on four occasions, by 50 basis points each time, since July 31 last year. The most recent cut was on May 23.
A Reuters survey of economists found that underlying inflation is expected to have risen by 0.4 percent in the June quarter, leading to an annual rate of 1.7 percent.
This would not only be below the RBA's two to three percent target band, but it would be the lowest the measure has been in the history of the Treasury series, which dates back to 1971.
The consumer price index (CPI) is expected to be flat in the quarter, with the annual CPI seen falling to a four-and-a-half year low of 0.6 percent.
Wages, a key determinant of underlying inflation, are expected to post quarterly growth of 0.8 percent.

Not only would this be the lowest quarterly growth in average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) for over a year, it would see the annual rate ease to 4.1 percent, away from the 4.5 percent level seen as the RBA's 'speed limit' on wages.

This combination is seen as bullish for an interest rate cut because it gives the RBA the room it needs to cut rates to help boost an economy currently running below capacity, with the weakness in employment growth and an unemployment rate stuck above 8.5 percent causing most concern.

"The soft patch in the economy appears to be continuing a little longer than we had anticipated. The now protracted fall in full-time employment is of particular concern," Rothschild Australia economists said in a commentary.
"In these circumstances, we feel the Bank will yield to the politicial and community pressure it currently faces."
A near term cut is seen as such a possibility that analysts are now talking about the size of the cut -- 50 basis points or 75 -- although most see it as the last in the current cycle.

"Rather like the last rate cut in the previous policy easing cycle in 1993, the next cash rate cut needs to be provide a psychological boost to sentiment in the economy, as well as evidently being the end of the easing process," UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said.
"What chance, therefore, of a 75 basis point cash rate cut, rather than a 50 basis point cut to finish the current rate cutting cycle?," he asked.

There are two dates that the market sees as possible alternatives for a rate cut announcement -- July 25 or August 6. The first date is the day after the release of the wages data and two days after the inflation data, while the latter date would be the morning after the next RBA board meeting.
Analysts were wary of ruling out one particular date, having been caught out by the timing of the last two rate cuts.
"We think the data is in place and they can cut any time," Westpac senior economist John Peters sid.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
